analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and Europe.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let Americans buy lower-priced prescription drugs from abroad, died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal law to let pharmacists, pharmacies, and wholesalers import prescription drugs from a list of developed countries with strong safety systems, and let individuals bring in up to a 90-day supply with a valid prescription. It required counterfeit-resistant packaging, surprise inspections of foreign sellers, and a public registry of approved exporters. It also made it illegal for drug manufacturers to raise prices abroad or cut off supplies to punish anyone who imported their drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, especially seniors and the uninsured, who could buy the same FDA-approved medicines from regulated pharmacies in Canada and Europe at far lower prices. US pharmacies and wholesalers that chose to import would also gain a new line of business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying out of pocket for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write rules permitting pharmacists, pharmacies, and wholesalers to import qualifying prescription drugs from a list of permitted countries including Canada, Japan, Australia, and the EU member states [S2].
Individuals could import a 90-day supply of a qualifying drug for personal use, with a valid prescription, from a licensed or registered internet pharmacy [S3].

The bill states that allowing open pharmaceutical markets could save American consumers at least $635 billion of their own money, and that Americans can pay up to 1,000 percent more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries [S3].

It would be unlawful for drug manufacturers to discriminate against importers, including charging them higher prices, restricting or delaying their supplies, or making products deliberately different abroad to block importation; violations would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, with triple damages available [S3].
Selling or importing a patented drug first sold abroad under the patent owner's authority would not count as patent infringement, removing a legal tool manufacturers used to block importation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose closed US market would open to competition from cheaper identical drugs sold in Canada and Europe. Inspection and registration costs would fall on exporters as fees [S2], and consumers would bear any residual safety risk from foreign-sourced drugs.

drawbacks.text: Safety depends entirely on enforcement: the bill relies on surprise inspections, counterfeit-resistant packaging, and a public registry of approved exporters to keep fake or substandard drugs out, and a badly enforced version of this system would put counterfeits in Americans' medicine cabinets [S3].

The bill excludes whole categories of expensive medicines, including biotechnology products, biologics, controlled substances, intravenous drugs, and drugs requiring refrigeration, so many of the costliest treatments would not qualify for importation [S3].

Manufacturers' most likely response is to restrict supply abroad or raise prices in Canada and Europe, a move the bill bans and threatens with enforcement, but policing foreign pricing decisions would be difficult in practice [S3].

Importation would expose consumers to counterfeit and mishandled drugs; the government has long had limited ability to verify the safety of medicines that enter outside official US distribution channels, which is why prior administrations of both parties hesitated to authorize it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: Americans pay the highest drug prices in the world, and this bill attacked the mechanism directly by opening regulated importation and punishing manufacturers who block it. The safety objection is real but was addressed with concrete machinery, surprise inspections, certified packaging, a public exporter registry, and tough enforcement. The bigger design limits are the exclusion of biologics and the fragility of relying on inspectors to police manufacturers' behavior in foreign markets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2009, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and stayed there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 6, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose exclusive, closed US market at the world's highest prices stayed intact. American consumers gained nothing; the gap the bill targeted remains.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the closed US market

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pharmaceutical Market Access Act of 2009, which would open US prescription drug markets to importation from developed countries.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for two years: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no report to the floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and allied patient groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed drug importation legislation, running safety-focused campaigns and lobbying against importation bills in this era, arguing foreign drugs could be counterfeit or unsafe.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. The sole sponsor was a Republican and not a single senator of either party cosponsored the bill, so the fight never took a partisan shape in the record.

industries.note: The bill opens their most profitable market to cheaper identical drugs from abroad and makes it unlawful to punish importers by raising foreign prices or cutting supplies. Their loss is consumers' price relief, which is why this industry has fought every version of importation legislation.

They would be authorized importers, able to buy qualifying drugs abroad and dispense them at lower cost, while being subject to the bill's testing and inspection rules. Their gain and the patient's savings point the same direction.

industries.industry: Foreign pharmacies and exporters in permitted countries
industries.note: Canadian, EU, and other registered exporters would gain legal access to US customers, subject to registration fees, surprise inspections, and counterfeit-resistant packaging requirements.
